questions.question: What does (\x -> x + 1) 5 evaluate to?
options: A type error — lambdas cannot be applied directly
questions.explanation: The lambda takes x, substitutes 5 for it, and computes 5 + 1 = 6. The parentheses around the lambda let it be applied immediately, just like a named function.
optionFeedback: Correct — substituting 5 for x gives 5 + 1 = 6.
That would be the value of x alone, but the body adds 1 to it before returning.
Lambdas can be applied directly as long as the whole lambda is parenthesised before the argument, exactly as written here.
That's the unevaluated body with x still a placeholder — applying the lambda substitutes the argument in and computes a number.

questions.question: Why does \x -> x + 1 5 (no parentheses around the lambda) fail to mean 'apply the lambda to 5'?
options: The lambda body extends as far right as possible, so this parses as \x -> (x + (1 5)), which tries to apply 1 to 5
Lambdas cannot take numeric arguments
-> must be followed immediately by a closing parenthesis
Backslash is reserved and cannot start an expression
questions.explanation: A lambda's body greedily extends to the right, so \x -> x + 1 5 is read as \x -> (x + (1 5)), which tries to apply the number 1 as if it were a function — a type error. Wrapping the lambda in parentheses, (\x -> x + 1) 5, fixes this by closing the body before the 5 arrives.
optionFeedback: Correct — without parentheses around the lambda, the whole tail belongs to its body, so 1 5 gets parsed as an application.
Lambdas take any kind of argument, including numbers — the issue here is purely about where the body ends, not what it accepts.
Nothing requires a closing parenthesis right after ->; the issue is that there is no parenthesis around the lambda at all.
Backslash is exactly how a lambda starts, and that part is fine — the problem is what happens after the arrow, not before it.

questions.question: Which pair of definitions mean exactly the same thing?
options: double x = x + x   and   double = \x -> x + x
double x = x + x   and   double = \x -> x
double = \x -> x + x   and   double x y = x + y
double x = x + x   and   double = x + x
questions.explanation: An equation f x = ... is shorthand for binding f to a lambda: f = \x -> .... Both forms describe exactly the same function value.
optionFeedback: Correct — the equation form and the lambda form describe the same function.
The right-hand side here drops the + x, so this lambda just returns its argument unchanged — not the same function as double.
The second definition takes two arguments and adds them; that's a different function from one that doubles a single argument.
double = x + x isn't a function at all — without a \x ->, x is an undefined free variable, not a parameter.

questions.question: Given add = \x -> (\y -> x + y), what is add 3 on its own?
options: A function that takes one more number and adds 3 to it
An error, because add needs two arguments
The number 3
A function that takes two more numbers
questions.explanation: add 3 substitutes 3 for x in the outer lambda, leaving \y -> 3 + y — a complete function value waiting for y. It is not an error and not yet a number.
optionFeedback: Correct — applying add to 3 returns the inner lambda with x fixed at 3.
Partial application is legal in Haskell; supplying fewer arguments than the full chain just returns the next function in the chain, not an error.
add 3 is a function value, not a number — you would need to apply it to a y to get a number back.
Only one more number is needed: the outer lambda already consumed x = 3, leaving just \y -> x + y waiting for y.

questions.question: let always5 = const 5. What does always5 "anything" return, and why?
options: 5, because const's inner lambda \_ -> x ignores its argument and returns the captured x
"anything", because always5 just echoes its input
A type error, because const expects two numbers
5, because const always evaluates its second argument first
questions.explanation: const x = \_ -> x. The wildcard pattern _ matches (and discards) whatever argument it is given, so the returned function always produces the x that was captured when const was first applied — here, 5.
optionFeedback: Correct — the wildcard discards the argument entirely, and the captured x = 5 is returned regardless of what comes in.
always5 discards whatever it's given — that's the entire point of const: the returned function ignores its argument.
const's second argument can be any type at all (it's the type variable b in a -> b -> a) — there is no numeric requirement here.
const doesn't evaluate its second argument at all; the wildcard pattern \_ never inspects it, so nothing is 'evaluated first'.

questions.question: Which of these actually uses its argument x, unlike const-style definitions that just discard it?
options: makeAdder n = \x -> x + n
makeAdder n = \_ -> n
makeAdder = \n x -> n
makeAdder n x = n
questions.explanation: makeAdder n = \x -> x + n captures n in a closure and returns a function whose body actually mentions its own argument x, unlike the other three, which all discard x and behave like const.
optionFeedback: Correct — the returned lambda uses both n (captured earlier) and x (its own argument).
This ignores x completely and always returns n — that is const's behaviour, not an adder.
Same issue: x is bound as a parameter but never used in the body, so this always returns n regardless of x.
Again x is never referenced on the right-hand side, so every call returns n unchanged — this is const in disguise.

deeper-reasoning-when-and-how-to-use-a-l.title: Deeper reasoning: when and how to use a lambda

questions.question: Two students write the same function, one with a where helper and one with a lambda. A reviewer asks which version should be preferred. Which answer gives the most balanced and accurate judgement?
options: The lambda version is always better, because it removes a name and shorter code is always more functional.
The where version is always better, because every function should have a name so that it can be tested.

The two versions compute the same list, [1,3,5,7,9]. The lambda puts a short, single-use rule where it is used and saves the reader a trip to find f. The named helper is better when the rule is complicated, is used more than once, or deserves an explanation. The choice is about clarity for this rule, not about one form being more functional than the other.
The two versions give different answers, because a lambda cannot see the value of n.
questions.explanation: A lambda is an anonymous function, and an equation with a name is shorthand for binding a name to one. The value they produce is identical. The decision is a readability judgement, and clarity comes before cleverness.
optionFeedback: Shorter is not automatically clearer. A long or reused rule is easier to understand with a name.

A name is useful for complicated rules, but a one-line rule used once does not become clearer by being named. Anything defined at the top level can also be tested whether or not a lambda is used inside it.
Correct. The two forms are interchangeable in meaning, and the decision depends on the rule's size and reuse.
The lambda in this example does not mention n at all. It receives each element of the range as its own argument x.

questions.question: A student writes the call below and GHC reports an unexpected lambda expression in function application. They try adding parentheses around the whole call, which does not help. Which explanation of the error, and which repair, is the most accurate?
options: A lambda cannot be passed to map; a named function must be defined first.

A lambda extends as far to the right as it can, and as an argument to another function it must be wrapped in parentheses so that its body stops where the lambda stops. Without them the tail [1, 2, 3] would be swallowed as part of the body, x * 2 [1, 2, 3]. The repair is map (\x -> x * 2) [1, 2, 3], which prints [2,4,6].
The problem is the multiplication, which has to be written as (*) x 2 inside a lambda.
The problem is that the list is missing its parentheses; (1, 2, 3) would be accepted.
questions.explanation: The greedy body is the reason that an applied or passed lambda needs brackets. The brackets mark the right-hand end of the lambda so that the list after it is a separate argument to map.
optionFeedback: Lambdas can be passed to map, and they often are. The problem is the missing brackets around this one.
Correct. The brackets around the lambda delimit its body, and the list then becomes the second argument to map.
Infix multiplication is allowed inside a lambda body. The error is about where the lambda ends.
Round brackets would make a tuple, which is a different type from a list and would not satisfy map.

questions.question: A student runs the program below and explains: "addFive remembers 5, but makeAdder 100 1 should not work, because I did not put brackets around makeAdder 100." Which explanation of the output corrects the claim and also separates makeAdder from const?
options: The program prints 15, then an error for makeAdder 100 1, because brackets are mandatory, then [2,3,4].

The program prints 15, 101 and [2,3,4]. Function application associates to the left, so makeAdder 100 1 already means (makeAdder 100) 1, and the brackets are optional. addFive keeps n = 5 inside the returned lambda, and unlike const, whose returned function ignores its argument, the lambda here uses both the remembered n and its own argument x.
The program prints 15, 101 and [1,2,3], because makeAdder only remembers its argument and never adds it.
The program prints 10, 1 and [1,2,3], because x is the only name used by the returned function.
questions.explanation: A multi-argument call is a chain of one-argument applications grouped from the left. The function returned by makeAdder captures n, which is what lets it behave differently for different arguments.
optionFeedback: Brackets are not required for makeAdder 100 1, because application groups to the left.
Correct. Left-grouping explains the unbracketed call, and the closure over n explains why the results depend on the first argument.
makeAdder adds its argument: the returned lambda computes x + n. The list is therefore [2,3,4].
The result of addFive 10 depends on n. It is 15, not 10.
